source_title: Politicians are afraid to fix taxes. So 100 citizens tried.
source_excerpt:
Embed Embed < iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6019535/nx-s1-mx-6019535-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Connecticut's property tax system has been broken for decades and the politicians have failed to fix the problem. So now, they're trying something new: a citizens assembly. (Citizens assemblies are also old. They go back to Ancient Greece, when lawmakers were chosen not through elections, but through random lotteries.)
Today on the show, Connecticut's citizens assembly. It's like jury duty, but for taxes. About hundred random people from all around Connecticut come together to try to solve the state's property tax problem. They wrestle with whether they should raise taxes, cut spending, find efficiencies, or a mix of everything. Will this alternative attempt to solve the unsolvable succeed, or will it be politics as usual?
It's a modern case study of what happens when politicians step aside to let citizens decide what's best. Come along as we talk to the professor who helped put this assembly together, learn from the citizens involved how this experiment changed them, and meet the politician who agreed to take their proposals to the state legislature.
